hops.afterHeading: One cell that ignores the world moving
hops.title: The frog fibers that ignored a whole meadow but not one speck
hops.text: In 1959, Jerome Lettvin and three colleagues at M.I.T. recorded single fibers in a frog's optic nerve and tried a low-budget test. They held a large color photograph of grass and flowers seven inches from the frog's eye and waved the whole picture around. One class of fibers gave no response at all. Then they stuck a fly-sized object to the photograph with a magnet and slid only that speck across the scene. The same fibers gave an excellent response, and they were tempted to call them bug perceivers. In the introduction, without reporting a feeding trial, they remarked that a frog will starve surrounded by motionless food.

sources.citation: Lettvin JY, Maturana HR, McCulloch WS, Pitts WH (1959), What the Frog's Eye Tells the Frog's Brain, Proceedings of the IRE 47:1940-1951

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A green frog on a lab bench watches a tiny bead on a large photograph of grass and flowers.
image.caption: Frog 'bug perceivers' ignored a whole waving meadow photo but answered one small speck sliding across it.

hops.afterHeading: Testing a type: agreement and a mosaic
hops.title: An adhesion molecule that keeps ganglion cells apart
hops.text: One molecule behind those regular mosaics has a misleading name: Down syndrome cell adhesion molecule, or DSCAM. Most mouse retinal ganglion cells make it. If DSCAM were simply glue, losing it should let cells drift apart. Peter Fuerst and colleagues found the opposite in mice lacking it. In several ganglion cell groups, cell bodies clumped and dendrites ran in bundles. In the alpha and melanopsin-positive ganglion cells examined for layering, dendrites still reached their usual broad regions of the inner plexiform layer. A 2009 commentary in Neuron summed it up in its title: mammalian DSCAMs won't help you find a partner, but they'll guarantee you some personal space.

sources.citation: Fuerst PG et al. (2009), DSCAM and DSCAML1 function in self-avoidance in multiple cell types in the developing mouse retina, Neuron 64(4):484-497 (PMID 19945391)
Fuerst PG, Koizumi A, Masland RH, Burgess RW (2008), Neurite arborization and mosaic spacing in the mouse retina require DSCAM, Nature 451(7177):470-474 (PMID 18216855)
Huberman AD (2009), Mammalian DSCAMs: they won't help you find a partner, but they'll guarantee you some personal space, Neuron 64(4):441-443 (PMID 19945385)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A microscope view of glowing golden neurons bunched into tight knots with bundled branches and empty gaps between them.
image.caption: Without DSCAM, several groups of mouse ganglion cells clump and bundle their dendrites instead of spacing out.

hops.afterHeading: Mouse is not macaque: the primate fovea
hops.title: Measuring your fovea with your thumbnail
hops.text: Hold your arm straight out and look at your thumbnail. That nail covers roughly the central two degrees of your view, about the patch your fovea serves. Now fix your gaze on one word here and try to read the words farther along the line: the farther they are from where you are looking, the harder they are to make out. In a scene, your eyes jump to a new spot about three times a second, bringing new patches into sharpest view. In a ring around the foveal center, human ganglion cells reach 32,000 to 38,000 per square millimeter. Farther out, midget ganglion cells pool signals from more cones.

sources.citation: Henderson JM, Hollingworth A (1999), High-level scene perception, Annual Review of Psychology 50:243-271
Curcio CA, Allen KA (1990), Topography of ganglion cells in human retina, Journal of Comparative Neurology 300(1):5-25 (PMID 2229487)
Kolb H, Marshak D (2003), The midget pathways of the primate retina, Documenta Ophthalmologica 106(1):67-81 (PMID 12675488)
